Blood tests and weight management: what they tell you | SHIFT
What blood tests can tell you about health and weight management, how to prepare and why the right investigations depend on your circumstances.

Blood tests can help investigate symptoms, assess particular health risks or monitor treatment. They cannot give every man a single explanation for why losing weight feels difficult. The appropriate tests depend on your health, medicines, history and the question being asked.

If you are losing weight without trying, speak to a GP rather than choosing a commercial panel to investigate it yourself. The [NHS advises getting continuing unintentional weight loss checked, especially when other symptoms are present](https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/unintentional-weight-loss/). You do not need to wait until you have lost a particular percentage.

## Start with the question, then consider the test

“I’m tired all the time” and “I want to understand my cardiovascular risk” are different starting points. Tell a healthcare professional what has changed, how long it has been happening and how it affects ordinary life.

[NICE’s adult weight-management guidance](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng246/chapter/Identifying-and-assessing-overweight-obesity-and-central-adiposity) says to consider other conditions and relevant previous assessments. It also warns against attributing every symptom to weight. That does not establish one compulsory blood-test bundle for every adult trying to lose weight.

Take a list of medicines and supplements, previous results if you have them, and a short symptom timeline. Ask what each proposed investigation could change about your care.

## What are the common areas a clinician may consider?

The following explains test categories. It is not a shopping list everyone needs to buy.

### Cholesterol and other blood fats

A lipid profile can inform a discussion about cardiovascular risk. High cholesterol usually has no symptoms, according to the [NHS cholesterol-testing guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-cholesterol/getting-tested/). A result may be useful alongside other risk information; it does not explain your motivation or prove why your weight has changed.

### Blood sugar

Blood glucose and HbA1c provide different information. HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly the previous two to three months, as described in [NHS type 1 diabetes information](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/type-1-diabetes/treatment/). It is not an instant picture of a rapidly changing problem. The appropriate test and interpretation belong with the clinician assessing you.

### Blood count and thyroid testing

The [NHS blood-test overview](https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/blood-tests/) explains that a full blood count measures blood cells, while thyroid testing can help investigate thyroid conditions. Their usefulness depends on the clinical question. Tiredness alone is not enough to identify which result, if any, will explain it.

### Liver and kidney markers

Check the exact markers included and what the report can tell you. “Liver function” and “kidney function” are headings for particular investigations, rather than guarantees that every possible problem has been excluded.

Kidney assessment can require urine testing as well as blood tests, as the [NHS kidney-disease guidance explains](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/kidney-disease/diagnosis/). A blood-only package is not the complete assessment for every concern.

### Vitamins, minerals and hormones

Ask why these are being measured and what would happen with the result. A longer list of markers does not automatically make a package more appropriate for you. Do not start hormone treatment or supplements because of an isolated number without suitable advice.

## Do I need to fast?

Follow the instructions for your particular test. Most people having a cholesterol test do not need to fast, although some are asked to. The NHS cholesterol page explains this distinction.

Check preparation, timing and medicines with the responsible service. Do not stop prescribed medicine on the strength of a generic internet checklist.

## How can samples be collected?

A professional venous sample is taken from a vein. Some home tests use a finger-prick sample. SHIFT is also trialling an upper-arm collection device as another proposed home option.

The sample method must be suitable for the tests being measured. It does not change the need for an appropriate panel, laboratory process and explanation of the report.

[Explore SHIFT Bloods](/shift-health/blood-tests) to compare the current proposals. Baseline and Advanced are being developed with two home collection options. Complete currently requires professional venous collection. The upper-arm device, final marker lists, prices and reporting arrangements are being confirmed. Ordering is closed.

## What should happen after a result?

Keep the complete report and ask who explains it, who arranges any follow-up and when you should hear back. A result needs to be considered alongside the reason for testing. If symptoms persist, return to that concern even if the report looks reassuring.

Testing is one possible part of looking after your health. Food, activity, sleep, mental health, medicines and existing conditions still deserve attention. You can take practical steps and ask for help without treating a commercial blood panel as an entry requirement.

*General information for UK adult readers; NICE recommendations cited concern adults in England’s guidance context. Independent clinical review is not claimed.*
Weight Loss Blood Tests for UK Men: 6 Checks, Results Explained
Learn which blood tests UK men can discuss with a GP, what common results may mean, and why symptoms and medical history matter beyond the numbers.

# Weight Loss Blood Tests for UK Men: 6 Checks, Results Explained

![Blood test tools framing a clean title area](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791981172108_Blood-test-tools-framing-a-clean-title-area.jpeg)

Clinicians commonly start with a thyroid test (TSH, often followed by free T4), a blood sugar check (HbA1c or glucose), a lipid profile, liver function tests and a full blood count with iron studies. These weight loss blood tests mostly rule things out and show your risk, rather than explain everything. If your weight has changed quickly or without trying, see your GP promptly.

***

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - Ask your GP to specify suspected pituitary disease because a TSH only request can miss it; free T4 usually follows an abnormal TSH.
> - HbA1c levels of 42–47 mmol/mol indicate prediabetes; 48 mmol/mol or higher is in the diabetic range, and asymptomatic results need repeat testing.
> - Unexplained weight loss of 5% or more over three months warrants prompt GP assessment, especially with persistent pain, signs of anemia, or worsening fatigue.
> - Suspected type 1 diabetes, particularly with severe thirst and frequent urination, calls for same day specialist referral rather than a routine appointment.
> - HbA1c reflects average blood sugar over roughly 6–8 weeks, so clinicians use glucose testing when high blood sugar develops quickly.

***

## Table of Contents

- [Which blood tests should you ask for?](#which-blood-tests-should-you-ask-for)
- [How do you read abnormal results?](#how-do-you-read-abnormal-results)
- [When should you see a GP urgently?](#when-should-you-see-a-gp-urgently)
- [How are blood tests done, and what can trip you up?](#how-are-blood-tests-done-and-what-can-trip-you-up)
- [Why blood tests are only the start](#why-blood-tests-are-only-the-start)
- [How can we help you take the next step?](#how-can-we-help-you-take-the-next-step)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Sources](#sources)

## Which blood tests should you ask for?

Think of this as a checklist you can take to your GP or a private clinic. Each test answers a different question.

- **TSH, then free T4.** TSH is the [primary thyroid screening test](https://laboratories.newcastle-hospitals.nhs.uk/test-directory/free-t4-serum/), and laboratories usually measure free T4 when TSH comes back abnormal. If your GP suspects a pituitary cause, the request has to say so, because a [TSH-only request can miss it](https://www.gloshospitals.nhs.uk/our-services/services-we-offer/pathology/tests-and-investigations/thyroid-function-tests-tsh-ft4-ft3/). Thyroid antibody testing may be added if TSH is mildly raised.
- **HbA1c or glucose.** These show how your body handles sugar. NICE advises [baseline checks of blood glucose or HbA1c](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-guide-for-prescribing-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-pdf-19828318651333) for anyone being assessed for overweight or obesity management.
- **Lipid profile.** Total cholesterol, HDL, LDL and triglycerides. This is about heart and metabolic risk, and NICE lists a fasting lipid profile in the same baseline set.
- **Liver function tests (LFTs).** These flag fatty liver disease, which is more likely with extra weight, type 2 diabetes or high blood pressure, and it can be present even when results look near normal. Kidney function is often checked alongside, mainly for medication safety.
- **Full blood count and iron studies.** These pick up anaemia or low iron, which can leave you drained and affect appetite.
- **Conditional extras.** Morning cortisol or sex hormones are usually only ordered when your history points towards an endocrine cause. Hormonal blood tests are rarely a first step on their own.

Many clinics bundle several of these into a single "weight management" or metabolic panel. A broader panel for unexplained weight loss can also include [CRP or ESR, a bone profile and kidney function](https://rmpartners.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/RDC-Investigating-weight-loss-March-2022.pdf), depending on your symptoms.

If you're comparing the best home blood tests in the UK, check which of the markers above each kit actually covers before you pay.

![Home finger-prick blood test kit components](https://media.babylovegrowth.ai/blog-images/organization-55073/1791981364975_Home-finger-prick-blood-test-kit-components.jpeg)

## How do you read abnormal results?

Results only make sense alongside your symptoms and history. Here is what the common patterns usually point to.

- **Thyroid.** A markedly raised TSH with a low free T4 suggests overt hypothyroidism. Typical symptoms are tiredness, feeling cold, constipation and weight gain. If you start treatment, TSH is rechecked [every 4–6 weeks](https://southwest.devonformularyguidance.nhs.uk/formulary/chapters/6-endocrine/management-of-thyroid-disorders/hypothyroidism) until it settles.
- **Blood sugar.** An HbA1c of 42–47 mmol/mol suggests pre-diabetes. A result of 48 mmol/mol or above falls in the diabetic range. Without symptoms, [a repeat test is advised to confirm](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/diagnostic-atlas-of-variation-education-toolkit/hba1c/?searchTerm=ovarian+cancer+referral+guidelines) the diagnosis.
- **Lipids.** High cholesterol or triglycerides tell you about long-term heart risk. They don't usually explain why the scales won't move.
- **Iron and haemoglobin.** Low levels can sap your energy and drive, which makes eating well and staying active harder.

A normal set of results doesn't close the case. Doctors also look at your medicines, mood, sleep and lifestyle, and may examine you or refer you on even when bloods are clear.

> **Blood sugar rule of thumb:** the pre-diabetes band runs from 42 to 47 mmol/mol, and 48 mmol/mol or above is the diabetic range, per [Right Decisions guidance](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/diagnostic-atlas-of-variation-education-toolkit/hba1c/?searchTerm=ovarian+cancer+referral+guidelines). Catching it in the pre-diabetes band gives you time to act.

## When should you see a GP urgently?

Don't wait for a routine slot if any of these apply. Unexplained weight loss of [5% or more over three months](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/nhs-tayside-refguide/cancer/non-specific-symptoms-of-cancer/) is the classic trigger for prompt assessment. Severe thirst with frequent urination, fast-worsening fatigue, signs of anaemia or new persistent pain also deserve quick attention. For suspected type 1 diabetes or rapid-onset symptoms, same-day specialist referral is the norm.

To make the appointment count, bring:

1. A simple timeline of your weight, with dates and rough figures.
2. Every medicine and supplement you take, including doses.
3. A short list of symptoms, such as thirst, tiredness, mood, sleep and appetite.
4. Any previous blood results you have.

## How are blood tests done, and what can trip you up?

Most tests use a venous blood draw at your surgery or a clinic. Home finger-prick kits can be convenient for some markers, but they don't cover everything a clinician may want to see.

- **Fasting.** Lipid profiles are usually done fasting. Follow the instructions you're given, drink water, and ask before skipping any regular medicine.
- **Timing.** Morning samples suit tests such as cortisol.
- **HbA1c limits.** It averages around 6–8 weeks, so it can miss fast-onset high blood sugar. In those cases clinicians go for [glucose-based testing](https://www.nbt.nhs.uk/sites/default/files/Diagnosis%20of%20Diabetes%20Mellitus%20%20%28BNSSG%29%20%282%29%20amended.pdf).
- **Interference.** Some drugs and supplements can [alter thyroid and other results](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/media/1575/central-hypothyroidism-primary-care.pdf), so declare everything.

**Pro Tip:** *Photograph your supplement labels before the appointment so nothing gets forgotten.*

## Why blood tests are only the start

Plenty of men want a single result that explains everything. In our experience of how this goes in practice, that rarely happens. NICE frames these checks as tools for [safe, evidence-based management and risk-stratification](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-guide-for-prescribing-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-pdf-19828318651333), not a "why can't I lose weight" verdict. The value is in finding treatable things early, such as an underactive thyroid or raised blood sugar, and in making sure any prescription is safe before it begins. Then comes the harder part: food, movement, mood and medication history, looked at together and followed up over months. A panel of results is a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it.

> *— Matt O’Brien*

If you want a clinician-led route rather than piecing it together alone, we can help. Our [Programme](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/programme) pairs clinically governed assessment with practical support for food, movement and goals, and our [weight-management medication pathway](https://shiftsometimber.co.uk/treatments/medication) is built around checks before anything is prescribed. Assessment and prescribing are carried out by appropriately regulated partners.

## FAQ

### Can the flu cause weight loss?

A bout of flu can cut your appetite for a few days and cause a small, temporary drop on the scales. That's usually fluid and missed meals rather than fat. If weight keeps falling after you recover, get it checked.

### What can cause weight loss without trying?

Common causes include an overactive thyroid, diabetes, digestive problems, low mood, and some medicines. Unexplained weight loss can also be a non-specific sign of cancer, which is why a GP review matters.

### Why do I feel colder after losing weight?

Less body fat means less insulation, and your body may also conserve energy when you eat less. If you feel cold alongside tiredness and constipation, ask for a thyroid test.

### Which blood tests are best for weight management?

Most clinicians start with TSH (with free T4), HbA1c or glucose, a lipid profile, liver function and a full blood count with iron studies. Extra tests depend on your symptoms and history.

Without symptoms, [a repeat test is advised to confirm](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/diagnostic-atlas-of-variation-education-toolkit/hba1c/?searchTerm=ovarian+cancer+referral+guidelines) the diagnosis. - **Lipids.** High cholesterol or triglycerides tell you about long-term heart risk. They don't usually explain why the scales won't move. - **Iron and haemoglobin.** Low levels can sap your energy and drive, which makes eating well and staying active harder. A normal set of results doesn't close the case. Doctors also look at your medicines, mood, sleep and lifestyle, and may examine you or refer you on even when bloods are clear. > **Blood sugar rule of thumb:** the pre-diabetes band runs from 42 to 47 mmol/mol, and 48 mmol/mol or above is the diabetic range, per [Right Decisions guidance](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/diagnostic-atlas-of-variation-education-toolkit/hba1c/?searchTerm=ovarian+cancer+referral+guidelines). Catching it in the pre-diabetes band gives you time to act. ## When should you see a GP urgently? Don't wait for a routine slot if any of these apply. Unexplained weight loss of [5% or more over three months](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/nhs-tayside-refguide/cancer/non-specific-symptoms-of-cancer/) is the classic trigger for prompt assessment. Severe thirst with frequent urination, fast-worsening fatigue, signs of anaemia or new persistent pain also deserve quick attention. For suspected type 1 diabetes or rapid-onset symptoms, same-day specialist referral is the norm. To make the appointment count, bring: 1. A simple timeline of your weight, with dates and rough figures. 2. Every medicine and supplement you take, including doses. 3. A short list of symptoms, such as thirst, tiredness, mood, sleep and appetite. 4. Any previous blood results you have. ## How are blood tests done, and what can trip you up? Most tests use a venous blood draw at your surgery or a clinic. Home finger-prick kits can be convenient for some markers, but they don't cover everything a clinician may want to see. - **Fasting.** Lipid profiles are usually done fasting. Follow the instructions you're given, drink water, and ask before skipping any regular medicine. - **Timing.** Morning samples suit tests such as cortisol. - **HbA1c limits.** It averages around 6–8 weeks, so it can miss fast-onset high blood sugar. In those cases clinicians go for [glucose-based testing](https://www.nbt.nhs.uk/sites/default/files/Diagnosis%20of%20Diabetes%20Mellitus%20%20%28BNSSG%29%20%282%29%20amended.pdf). - **Interference.** Some drugs and supplements can [alter thyroid and other results](https://www.rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk/media/1575/central-hypothyroidism-primary-care.pdf), so declare everything. **Pro Tip:** *Photograph your supplement labels before the appointment so nothing gets forgotten.* ## Why blood tests are only the start Plenty of men want a single result that explains everything. In our experience of how this goes in practice, that rarely happens. NICE frames these checks as tools for [safe, evidence-based management and risk-stratification](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta1026/resources/a-guide-for-prescribing-medicines-to-manage-overweight-and-obesity-pdf-19828318651333), not a "why can't I lose weight" verdict. The value is in finding treatable things early, such as an underactive thyroid or raised blood sugar, and in making sure any prescription is safe before it begins. Then comes the harder part: food, movement, mood and medication history, looked at together and followed up over months. A panel of results is a starting point for that conversation, not a replacement for it. > *— Matt O’Brien* ## How can we help you take the next step? Consult a qualified healthcare professional about your own circumstances before acting on anything here. ## FAQ ### Can the flu cause weight loss? A bout of flu can cut your appetite for a few days and cause a small, temporary drop on the scales. That's usually fluid and missed meals rather than fat. If weight keeps falling after you recover, get it checked. ### What can cause weight loss without trying? Common causes include an overactive thyroid, diabetes, digestive problems, low mood, and some medicines. Unexplained weight loss can also be a non-specific sign of cancer, which is why a GP review matters. ### Why do I feel colder after losing weight? Less body fat means less insulation, and your body may also conserve energy when you eat less. If you feel cold alongside tiredness and constipation, ask for a thyroid test. ### Which blood tests are best for weight management? Most clinicians start with TSH (with free T4), HbA1c or glucose, a lipid profile, liver function and a full blood count with iron studies.
